read.sections.0.heading.source: A place and a turning point
read.sections.0.heading.back: A place and a turning point

read.sections.0.text.source: On 15 February 1942, British forces surrendered to Japanese forces at the Ford Factory in Singapore. This began the Japanese occupation, which lasted until 1945. Today the factory holds an exhibition about the war, run by the National Archives of Singapore. During the occupation, everyday routines changed. Many schools closed or were used for other things, and many children lost time in class. People did not all live through the same events in the same way. A photo of the building today can show us a place. It cannot show us how people lived there in 1942.
read.sections.0.text.back: On 15 February 1942, British forces surrendered to Japanese forces at the Ford Factory in Singapore. This event began the Japanese Occupation, which lasted until 1945. Today, the factory houses an exhibition about the war, run by the National Archives of Singapore. During the occupation, daily routines changed. Many schools closed or were used for other things, and many children lost learning time in class. Not everyone went through the same events in the same way. A photo of the building today can show us a place. The photo cannot show how people lived there in 1942.

read.sections.0.simpler.source: On 15 February 1942, British forces gave up Singapore. Japanese forces took control. This was the start of the Japanese occupation. It lasted until 1945. The British gave up in a factory. Today the building has a show about the war. Daily life changed in this time. Many schools closed. Many children missed school. People had different lives. A photo of the building today shows a place. It does not show how people lived in 1942.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: On 15 February 1942, British forces handed over Singapore. Japanese forces took over. This was the start of the Japanese Occupation. This occupation lasted until 1945. The British gave up at a factory. Today the building has an exhibition about the war. Daily life changed at this time. Many schools closed. Many children could not go to school. Each person went through a different life. A photo of the building today shows a place. The photo does not show how people lived in 1942.

read.sections.1.text.source: Singapore's Ministry of Education Heritage Centre writes about schools in this time. It says the Japanese military government made Japanese lessons compulsory in schools in 1942. Teachers had to learn Japanese, and they could not use English in school. There was a shortage of food, so many schools grew their own. Gardening became part of lessons. Tapioca, a root that grows easily, became an important food. This source tells us about rules and examples of school life. It does not tell us that every child went to school or had the same lessons. For most children, school almost stopped.
read.sections.1.text.back: The MOE Heritage Centre, the heritage centre of Singapore's Ministry of Education, writes about schools at this time. According to it, the Japanese military government made Japanese lessons compulsory in schools in 1942. Teachers had to learn Japanese, and they could not use English at school. There was a shortage of food, so many schools grew their own food. Gardening became part of lessons. Cassava, a kind of root that grows easily, became an important food. This source tells us about rules and examples of school life. It does not tell us that every child went to school or got the same lessons. For most children, schooling almost stopped.
read.sections.1.text.note: "Tapioca, a root that grows easily" became "Ubi kayu, sejenis ubi yang mudah tumbuh" (cassava, a kind of tuber that grows easily).

read.sections.1.simpler.source: A history centre in Singapore writes about schools in this time. It says Japanese lessons were compulsory from 1942. Teachers had to learn Japanese. There was a shortage of food. So many schools grew food. Tapioca is a root plant that grows easily. It became an important food. This source shows us rules. It does not show that every child went to school.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: A history centre in Singapore writes about schools at this time. According to it, Japanese lessons were compulsory from 1942. Teachers had to learn Japanese. There was a shortage of food. So many schools grew food. Cassava is a kind of root that grows easily. It became an important food. This source shows us rules. This source does not show that every child went to school.

read.sections.2.text.source: Before the war, Singapore bought most of its food from other places. The war cut the ships and trains that brought rice. Lee Geok Boi wrote about wartime food for the National Library in 2019. She used oral history interviews. She explains that every home needed a ration card, and the rice ration got smaller over time. Many people ate tapioca and sweet potatoes instead of rice. Some food was sold in secret at very high prices, so people with more money could get more. For most people, meals were not enough to stay healthy. To learn about meals then, we need food records or memories, not a photo of the factory now.
read.sections.2.text.back: Before the war, Singapore bought most of its food from other places. The war cut the ship and train routes that brought rice. Lee Geok Boi wrote about wartime food for Singapore's National Library in 2019. She used oral history interviews. She explains that every home needed a ration card, and the rice ration got smaller over time. Many people ate cassava and sweet potatoes in place of rice. Some food was sold secretly at very high prices, so people with more money could get more. For most people, their food was not enough to stay healthy. To learn about meals at that time, we need food records or people's memories, not a photo of the factory today.

read.sections.2.simpler.source: Before the war, most food came to Singapore by ship. The war stopped much of the rice. Lee Geok Boi wrote about this in 2019. She used oral history. Each home needed a ration card. Over time, the rice ration got smaller. Many people ate tapioca and sweet potatoes. Some food was sold in secret, for a lot of money. Most people did not get enough food to stay healthy. The photo of the factory does not show what people ate.
read.sections.2.simpler.back: Before the war, most food reached Singapore by ship. The war stopped much of the rice supply. Lee Geok Boi wrote about this in 2019. She used oral history. Every home needed a ration card. Over time, the rice ration got smaller. Many people ate cassava and sweet potatoes. Some food was sold secretly, at a high price. Most people did not have enough to eat to stay healthy. The photo of the factory does not show what people ate.

watch.summary.source: This video is part of a cooking show from Singapore's National Library. A librarian and a guest cook, Lee Geok Boi, make food from the time of the Japanese occupation. First, they talk about the past. There was a shortage of rice in the war. So people ate tapioca and sweet potatoes instead. Tapioca was easy to grow. The video also talks about rations, and about food that was sold in secret for a lot of money. Then Lee Geok Boi cooks two dishes. She uses only foods that people could get at the time. She makes noodles from tapioca and sweet potato. She also makes boiled tapioca with coconut. The video says tapioca fills you up, but it does not give the body all it needs to stay healthy.
watch.summary.back: This video is part of a cooking show by Singapore's National Library. A librarian and a guest cook, Lee Geok Boi, prepare food from the time of the Japanese Occupation. First, they talk about the past. During the war there was a shortage of rice. So people ate cassava and sweet potatoes instead. Cassava was easy to grow. The video also talks about rations, and about food that was sold secretly at a high price. Then Lee Geok Boi cooks two dishes. She uses only ingredients that could be got at that time. She makes noodles from cassava and sweet potato. She also makes boiled cassava with coconut. The video says cassava fills you up, but it does not give the body everything it needs to stay healthy.

sensitiveNotes.0.source: This lesson is about a wartime occupation, and some learners have lived through war, conflict or displacement. Never ask learners about their own or their family's experiences of war or displacement, or about their home country, religion or ethnicity, and never ask them to compare their lives with the people in the sources. Keep the discussion on the sources about school and food, and let any learner step out without giving a reason. The lesson needs no violent images. The occupation also brought killings and harsh punishments; the lesson does not describe them and you do not need to. If learners raise them, say plainly that many people were harmed, then return to the sources. Preview before sharing: the NLB article mentions a harsh punishment in one line, and the video may show photos of starving prisoners of war (from 5:04).
sensitiveNotes.0.back: This lesson is about an occupation during war, and some learners have been through war, conflict or having to leave their homes. Never ask learners about their own or their family's experiences of war or displacement, or about their home country, religion or ethnicity, and never ask them to compare their lives with the people in these sources. Keep the discussion on the sources about school and food, and let any learner leave without giving a reason. This lesson needs no pictures of violence. The occupation also brought killings and cruel punishments; the lesson does not describe them and you do not need to describe them. If learners mention them, say clearly that many people suffered, then return to the sources. Check first before sharing: the NLB article mentions one cruel punishment in one line, and the video may show photos of starving prisoners of war (from 5:04).
sensitiveNotes.0.note: "many people were harmed" rendered "ramai orang menderita" (many people suffered); "ramai orang dicederakan" is more literal. "step out" rendered "keluar" (leave the discussion/room): reviewer to check it reads as stepping out of the discussion, not being sent out.
